parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A rock of mass $7.5\text{ kg}$ is projected vertically upwards from the surface of a planet. The rock leaves the surface of the planet with a speed of $4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t = 0$. The variation with time $t$ of the velocity $v$ of the rock is shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1

Assume that the planet does not have an atmosphere and that the viscous force acting on the rock is always zero.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Determine the height of the rock above the surface of the planet at time $t = 4.0\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the change in the momentum of the rock from time $t = 0$ to time $t = 4.0\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the weight $W$ of the rock on this planet.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
In practice, the planet in (b) does have an atmosphere that causes a viscous force to act on the moving rock.

State and explain the variation, if any, in the resultant force acting on the rock as it moves vertically upwards.

markscheme_points.text: speed/velocity decreases so viscous force decreases
viscous force decreases (and weight constant) so resultant force decreases

hints: As the rock rises, its upward speed falls, while its weight remains constant.
The viscous force opposes the upward motion, so combine it with the downward weight when considering the resultant force.
walkthrough: While the rock moves upwards, its speed decreases.
The downward viscous force decreases as the speed decreases, but the downward weight is constant.
The downward resultant force is weight plus viscous force, so its magnitude decreases as the rock rises.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: Height is determined geometrically from the area under the velocity-time graph (area of triangle from t=0 to 2.5s minus area from t=2.5 to 4.0s).

hints: The displacement from a velocity-time graph is the signed area between the graph and the time axis.
From 0 to 4.0 s, separate the positive triangle above the axis from the negative triangle below it.
walkthrough: Height above the surface is the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s, found from the signed area under the velocity-time graph.
The graph reaches v = −2.4 m s⁻¹ at 4.0 s, so the area below the time axis must be subtracted.
Positive area = ½ × 2.5 s × 4.0 m s⁻¹ = 5.0 m; negative area magnitude = ½ × 1.5 s × 2.4 m s⁻¹ = 1.8 m.
Displacement = 5.0 − 1.8 = 3.2 m, so the rock is 3.2 m above the surface.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the signed area under the velocity-time graph to determine displacement.
Reads the velocity at 4.0 s as −2.4 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts the 1.8 m negative triangular area from the 5.0 m positive triangular area to obtain a height of 3.2 m.

hints: Take upward velocity as positive, so the velocity at 4.0 s has a negative sign.
For a constant mass, calculate change in momentum from m(v − u).
walkthrough: Take upward as positive. The initial velocity is u = +4.0 m s⁻¹ and the graph gives v = −2.4 m s⁻¹ at 4.0 s.
For constant mass, change in momentum is Δp = m(v − u).
The negative sign shows that the momentum change is downward.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the mass with the signed velocity change, 7.5[−2.4 − 4.0].
Obtains a momentum change of −48 N s.

hints: With no atmosphere, weight is the only force on the rock and causes its momentum to change.
Use the 48 N s momentum-change magnitude from part (ii) over 4.0 s, or find the acceleration from the change in velocity.
walkthrough: With no viscous force, the resultant force is the rock's weight.
Using force as rate of change of momentum, W = |Δp| / Δt = 48 / 4.0 = 12 N.
Equivalently, the acceleration magnitude is |−2.4 − 4.0| / 4.0 = 1.6 m s⁻², so W = ma = 7.5 × 1.6 = 12 N.
This is also W = mg with g = 1.6 N kg⁻¹ on the planet.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses either force as rate of momentum change or an equivalent weight relationship such as W = ma or W = mg.
Uses the 4.0 s interval with the 48 N s momentum-change magnitude, or an acceleration magnitude of 1.6 m s⁻², to obtain W = 12 N.
